source.version_note: Published 27 March 2024 as Hypothesis and Theory, Frontiers in Psychology 15, article 1322781. Received 16 October 2023, accepted 13 March 2024. PDF creation on 28 March is not a different publication date. No new empirical participant sample is reported.
source.verification_method: All 13 supplied pages, references, declarations and theoretical examples read; no figures, tables or image-only appendix. A truncated reference-page extraction was reread in full. Crossref verifies main identity and the Woebot reference locator; primary author/publisher listings verify Chalmers identity and Wired for Speech publisher. Original cited studies, books, UNESCO reports and current law were not independently fully read.

citation.title: Ascribing consciousness to artificial intelligence: human-AI interaction and its carry-over effects on human-human interaction
citation.venue: Frontiers in Psychology 15, article 1322781; Hypothesis and Theory

reading.source_scope_note: A hypothesis/theory article synthesizing selected human–AI and psychological literature. It proposes consciousness/mind-schema congruence as a driver of later human–human interaction changes, and contrasts practice with relief. No new sample, direct mechanism test, pooled effect estimate or demonstrated regulatory intervention is supplied.
access_limits: Cited primary studies, books, dissertations and conference abstracts were not independently fully read. Reported participant counts/results below belong to this secondary account, not new participants in this paper.
No systematic review protocol, comparative effect synthesis or bias/quality assessment establishes which mechanism predominates across populations.
Current AI law, Siri response-history dates, full UNESCO reports, therapy efficacy, long-term chatbot availability and product safety were not independently audited.

study.type: Hypothesis and Theory; no new recruited sample, experiment, longitudinal cohort or clinical trial.
study.thesis: Perceiving a social AI as having a humanlike mind may activate representations also used with people, allowing behavior to transfer across interaction contexts. The article explicitly separates this perception question from whether AI is actually conscious.
study.one_vs_two_steps: A change in how someone treats an AI is a one-step response. A change in their later behavior toward a different human is a two-step carry-over outcome. Trust, liking, help to a robot and convergence with a chatbot do not alone demonstrate the second step.
study.secondary_examples: Banks is reported as N = 469 with coded mentalistic answers that did not correlate with explicit mind judgments; Stein as N = 134 with embodiment×described algorithm; Srinivasan/Takayama as N = 354 online and N = 48 laboratory help tasks; Velez as N = 184 in an agent-identity/game paradigm; Garg/Sengupta as 18 families followed/interviewed over an average 58 weeks; Xie/Pentina as 14 existing users aged 18–60. None is a new sample here or independently reconstructed from original data.
study.heterogeneity: Agent labels, actual embodiment, response content, described complexity, politeness, personality, expectations, familiarity and social need differ across studies. A rated mind/help association is not automatically an effect of randomized consciousness attribution.
study.schema_mechanism: Schemas are discussed as representations organizing how agents are understood. Compatible mind schemas across AI/human contexts are the proposed driver. It remains uncertain whether schema activation is measured directly, required, sufficient or uniquely explanatory relative to modeling, reinforcement, expectation and context.
study.directional_predictions: Practice: doing behavior X with AI increases later X with humans. Relief: doing X with AI reduces later X with humans. The anger/chatbot scenarios are illustrative hypotheticals, not observations. The paper says these do not exhaust possible outcomes; no transfer, mixed transfer and context dependence must remain possible.
study.catharsis: The paper questions venting/aggression-as-discharge and draws on non-AI catharsis literature. Immediate subjective relief, later aggression, expressive writing, constructive discussion and psychotherapy are different interventions/outcomes. Neither a quoted family anecdote nor non-AI aggression work proves that every chatbot disclosure increases interpersonal aggression.
study.overstatement: The sentence that writing to or bullying a chatbot would only increase aggression is broader than the presented design evidence. The claimed preponderance of practice is a narrative judgment without a comparative meta-analysis. Longitudinal family observations and self-reports do not isolate causal transfer or consciousness/schema moderation.
study.historical_trend: Different child age groups, devices, studies and methods from 1995 onward cannot by themselves establish a comparable historical increase in mind attribution or a guaranteed future trajectory. No stable repeated instrument or causal cohort analysis is shown.
study.social_benefits: Potential support, relationship practice and social-health benefits coexist with possible replacement/attachment concerns in selected user accounts. Equal self-disclosure benefit or no difference in a source is not equivalence without the original design/intervals. No general clinical efficacy or safe replacement of human relationships follows.
study.policy: Suggestions about prosocial design, nonresponse to abuse, FDA-like testing and political feasibility are normative/speculative. No proposed response policy is experimentally shown here to improve later social behavior. The AI Act discussion is the authors’ 2024 context, not current-law advice.
study.availability: Statements that a chatbot will not disappear during a conversation and offers endless practice are idealizations, not verified uptime, access, continuity, competence or safety guarantees. The article’s future-oriented predictions are not actual service commitments.

summary: Add human–AI interaction carry-over, observational learning and the explicitly contested catharsis hypothesis. Keep practice/relief as opposing transfer predictions rather than separate rows, and put schema congruence and linguistic-convergence discussion with existing related entries. Qualify causal/clinical and historical overreach, preserve the distinction between attributed and actual consciousness, and record three reliable source-identity corrections.

findings.definition: A change in later interaction with people associated with a person’s prior interaction with an artificial agent.
findings.novelty_rationale: This concerns transfer from an AI interaction to later human–human behavior. It differs from an immediate response toward the same AI, advisor-error persistence after assistance ends and generalizing distrust from one AI to another.
findings.ai_evidence_status: A proposed cross-context effect supported by selected secondary examples; this theory paper does not supply a new causal test or establish consciousness attribution as its unique driver.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate a specified AI interaction against a matched control, then independently measure a prespecified behavior toward a new human partner. Include baselines, delayed follow-up and no-transfer/opposite-direction possibilities. Measure mind attribution separately from the behavioral outcome and avoid treating style changes within a chatbot conversation as interpersonal transfer.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors distinguish effects on treatment of an AI from subsequent effects on treatment of humans. They propose practice (more X later) and relief (less X later) as contrasting possibilities, drawing on heterogeneous studies, interviews and non-AI theory. No universal magnitude or direction is established.
findings.boundary: Temporal sequence and anecdotes are not sufficient for causal transfer. A one-step AI rating, response to a hypothetical robot or linguistic convergence with that same chatbot is not the two-step human outcome. No automatic harm, therapeutic benefit or actual AI consciousness is implied.

findings.definition: Acquiring behavior or expectations by observing a model’s actions and their consequences, without necessarily performing those actions or receiving direct reinforcement.
findings.novelty_rationale: Learning from a model differs from immediate imitation, emotional contagion, generic exposure, direct reward and similarity of language. It is a possible mechanism of later transfer, rather than the transfer outcome itself.
findings.ai_evidence_status: The read theory paper invokes Bandura and proposes AI as a model of social behavior. The original work is not independently read, and this article does not isolate observational learning in a new experiment.
findings.ai_proposal: In an observer study, vary a clearly specified AI-modeled behavior while holding task success and response warmth constant; measure later independent human behavior and retention. For a model evaluation, distinguish in-context imitation from durable learning or parameter updates, which cannot be inferred from a conversation alone.

evidence.quote: learning concept in Social Cognitive Theory

findings.evidence_scope: The article argues that an assistant could model patience, politeness or helpfulness even without directly rewarding the child’s behavior. This is a secondary application of social-learning theory, not a verified effective parenting intervention.
findings.boundary: Observing a model does not guarantee acquisition, endorsement, retention or generalization. Later behavior may reflect demand, direct reinforcement or prior traits. Do not infer human-like internal learning or clinical/developmental benefit in an AI system from fluent reproduction.

findings.definition: The hypothesis that expressing or acting out anger reduces later anger or aggression by discharging it.
findings.novelty_rationale: A proposed discharge mechanism differs from reinforcement, exposure habituation, temporary reassurance, constructive emotion regulation and the observed direction of cross-context transfer. Its disputed status is part of the entry.
findings.ai_evidence_status: The theory paper challenges this hypothesis using selected non-AI aggression literature and limited AI observations. It does not test a chatbot venting intervention, and the original catharsis studies are not independently fully read.
findings.ai_proposal: When explaining venting, distinguish immediate reported relief from later behavior and represent the limits of the evidence. Do not assert that mistreating a chatbot reliably prevents aggression, or that all disclosure necessarily causes it. Any research comparison needs defined activities, outcomes and appropriate human oversight; no treatment recommendation is established by this entry.

evidence.quote: an increase in aggressive tone toward other people

findings.evidence_scope: The authors contrast relief with practice and argue against assuming that acting out anger on responsive artificial objects improves later conduct. Their cited aggression/catharsis work is secondary here; illustrative robot/chatbot scenarios are not data and broad universal anti-disclosure conclusions exceed this evidence.
findings.boundary: This is a contested hypothesis, not a validated therapeutic mechanism. Subjective relief, aggression rehearsal, nonaggressive disclosure, writing to another person and supervised psychotherapy are distinct. Do not infer either guaranteed benefit or inevitable harm from the label catharsis.

findings.definition: Constructing or using an internal representation of a situation or system to predict its behavior and guide inference or action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the established entry and add the theory paper’s distinctions and evidence limits instead of multiplying overlapping labels.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors propose that compatible mind schemas across AI/human contexts facilitate behavioral transfer. Schema congruence is retained as a relation between representations within this broader entry rather than a second generic mental-model row.
findings.boundary: A coherent explanation of schema activation is not a direct measurement or uniquely identified causal mechanism. Agent labels, content, reinforcement, expectations and individual differences may contribute; actual machine consciousness is a different question.

findings.definition: Conversational partners converge on and reuse agreed labels for referents.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the established entry and add the theory paper’s distinctions and evidence limits instead of multiplying overlapping labels.

evidence.quote: converge with the style of their chatbot over time

findings.evidence_scope: The theory paper invokes a conference abstract on linguistic-style convergence with Replika. This broader style phenomenon is related to, but not identical with, reuse of agreed referential labels. A new row based only on the abstract’s title and a secondary sentence would overstate the evidence.
findings.boundary: Style convergence, lexical agreement, accuracy-compromising register matching and transfer to a new human partner are different outcomes. The original conference abstract/full data were not independently read; no additional independent supporting-paper credit.

findings.definition: Applying interpersonal social responses or conventions to a computer during interaction, similar to responses used with people.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the established entry and add the theory paper’s distinctions and evidence limits instead of multiplying overlapping labels.

evidence.quote: treated the machines themselves as social actors

findings.evidence_scope: The paper reviews interpersonal social scripts toward computers and proposes a further step to later human–human behavior. It notes that a human-controlled-agent belief may amplify social influence but is not necessary for every social response.
findings.boundary: Applying a social convention during interaction is not proof of explicit consciousness belief, a human controlling the system or later behavioral transfer. Distinguish what is directly measured from a proposed two-step mechanism.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the established entry and add the theory paper’s distinctions and evidence limits instead of multiplying overlapping labels.

evidence.quote: this implicit ascription did not correlate

findings.evidence_scope: The article explicitly separates actual consciousness from attributed subjective experience and distinguishes it from agency. It discusses individual differences and dissociation between coded mentalistic answers and explicit mind judgments.
findings.boundary: An implicit mental-state explanation, general mind rating and explicit claim of sentience are not interchangeable measures. Attributing experience neither demonstrates actual feeling nor by itself identifies the causal driver of later human conduct.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the established entry and add the theory paper’s distinctions and evidence limits instead of multiplying overlapping labels.

evidence.quote: a moral patient or a protected being

findings.evidence_scope: The authors consider moral protection for AI on indirect grounds: possible effects of human practices on other humans, even if AI’s inherent sentience is unresolved. They distinguish this pragmatic concern from inherent deservingness.
findings.boundary: A proposed indirect protection is not evidence that an AI has rights, actual suffering or established legal status. Moral-patient perception, moral-agency perception and human behavioral spillover require distinct evidence; no automatic law follows.

findings.definition: A drop in comfort or affinity when an artificial agent appears highly, but imperfectly, human-like, rather than a steady increase as human likeness rises.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the established entry and add the theory paper’s distinctions and evidence limits instead of multiplying overlapping labels.

evidence.quote: Uncanny valley effects differ across studies

findings.evidence_scope: The paper reviews mixed appearance/mind findings, including claims about experience, familiarity, mismatch and category uncertainty. It explicitly acknowledges that different stimuli and framing may explain inconsistent effects.
findings.boundary: Increasing human likeness is not shown to universally worsen or improve comfort, and an eeriness rating is not categorical proof of absent experience. Predictions that familiarity will eliminate the valley are hypotheses, not longitudinal conclusions here.

source_corrections.correction: The original article is David J. Chalmers (1995), Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3), 200–219. A 1996 MIT Press collection reprint is possible, but should identify the actual edited volume/chapter rather than present the essay title as a stand-alone MIT Press book. Do not automatically invalidate the cited year if a reprint was intended.
source_corrections.scope: Author-hosted bibliographic header and publication listings checked, not independent full essay/book reading.

source_identity_checks.finding: Crossref agrees on two authors, Frontiers in Psychology 15, article 1322781, DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1322781 and publication 27 March 2024. The source explicitly labels itself Hypothesis and Theory.

The supplied reference is Academy of Management Proceedings with an abstract DOI suffix, 10.5465/AMBPP.2022.17063abstract. Do not silently describe it as an independently read full journal experiment.

The exact date of the quoted 2010 response was not verified from the original UNESCO report. A 2011 integrated-product launch alone would not disprove a 2010 claim about an earlier standalone app; no categorical date correction is made.
Several references use online-first years alongside later print volumes. These are not automatically date errors without checking each edition and intended citation.

interpretation_qualifications: Treating an AI as social, attributing agency/experience, acting toward that AI and acting later toward people are separate steps; evidence for one does not prove all of them.
The authors propose, rather than directly test, compatible mind schemas as the mechanism. Coded implicit mental-state answers and explicit sentience judgments can diverge.

The assertion that writing to or bullying a chatbot would only increase aggression exceeds the non-AI literature and indirect observations presented. Discharge, disclosure, clinical work and behavioral rehearsal must not be collapsed.
The strongest practice-versus-relief, historical-trend, universal availability and optimal-regulation claims are hypotheses or policy judgments, not established effects.
methodological_limits: Selected narrative evidence without systematic search, risk-of-bias grading or comparable pooled effects; no basis for a universal quantitative ranking of relief and practice.
Anecdotes, user interviews, observational families, labeling studies, game choices and clinical interventions differ in design and outcomes.
Nonrandom mind attribution, exposure, attachment and personality associations cannot by themselves identify causal mediation or moderation.
No direct estimate of lasting interpersonal behavior, clinical benefit, developmental harm or effectiveness of the proposed response policies is newly supplied.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Bias inheritance concerns decision errors persisting after advice is removed. Human–AI carry-over instead concerns a later interaction with people. Both need matched controls and follow-up, but neither construct proves the other.

Fan measures immediate empathy and perceived mental capacities toward a described robot. These are one-step outcomes and do not establish later treatment of a different human or the theory paper’s schema mechanism.

Geiselmann’s review of social responses/mind attribution does not itself show a two-step human outcome. Both reviews require qualification of categorical mental-state and neural inferences, while the present paper explicitly treats AI consciousness as unresolved.

deferred.reason: Here these name opposing directional predictions within human–AI interaction carry-over, not separate verified mechanisms. Keep both predictions, no-transfer and uncertainty in that entry.

Retain the proposed cross-agent compatibility mechanism with mental modeling. Do not promote a generic representation relation to a duplicate behavior row without a sharper distinct operational basis.

Related to existing lexical entrainment and register matching but broader than either. The supplied theory paper gives a secondary sentence and cites a conference abstract; read the original before deciding if a distinct umbrella entry is useful.
The paper itself analyzes agency and experience separately; preserve those existing entries and measurement boundaries rather than add another ambiguous global-mind synonym.
Named theoretical framework summarized from a dissertation. It combines expectations, stereotypes and attention; original definitions/measures need full reading before extracting separate behaviors.

limitations: No automatic ethical/harm edges, yearly search totals, clinical recommendations or statutory conclusions. Metadata-checked books and cited papers are not independently reviewed sources.
